title: Treaty, Convention and Protocol
canonical_question: Write short notes on Treaty, Convention and Protocol.
present_day_examinable_core: The TAXONOMY of international instruments - what each of the three words denotes, how they relate to one another, and what each does in the IMO system. A distinct examinable task from the PROCESS by which an IMO convention is adopted and enters into force.

recommended_exam_depth.note: MIW's recommendation for one limb of a four-limb 'write short notes on any THREE' question. The sittings that evidence this family print a paper total only, with no per-question or per-limb split.

understand_first: The trap in this limb is that the three words are not three parallel things. Treaty is the generic legal category; convention and protocol are both treaties, distinguished by the job they do rather than by their legal force. Once that hierarchy is stated the rest of the answer writes itself, and an answer that opens with it has already earned most of the limb. The second thing worth seeing is why protocols exist at all in the IMO system. A convention that has entered into force is extremely hard to reopen, because reopening it means every State party has to consent again and the instrument can stall for a decade. A protocol is the device that lets the Organization change or extend an instrument without that. MARPOL is the standing example: the 1973 Convention never entered into force on its own and was rescued by being absorbed into the 1978 Protocol - which is why the instrument is properly cited as MARPOL 73/78 and not as MARPOL 1973.

blocks.p: A treaty is the general term in international law for a binding agreement between States. The Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, 1969 defines it in Article 2(1)(a) as an international agreement concluded between States in written form and governed by international law, whatever its particular designation. That last phrase is the point of the definition: the NAME does not determine the legal character. A convention, a protocol, an agreement, a charter and a covenant are all treaties, and all bind a State that has consented to be bound by them.

A treaty binds only those States that have consented to be bound - by ratification, acceptance, approval or accession, evidenced by depositing an instrument with the depositary. Adoption of the text creates no obligation on any State.

A convention is a multilateral treaty, usually negotiated and adopted at a diplomatic conference, that establishes a substantial body of law on a subject. In the IMO system the conventions are the primary instruments: SOLAS 1974, MARPOL, STCW 1978, Load Lines 1966, COLREG 1972, MLC 2006 (adopted by the ILO), the Salvage Convention 1989, and so on.
Two features are worth stating because they are what the examiner is testing:

ul: A convention carries its own entry-into-force conditions. These are written into the instrument, typically a minimum number of contracting States representing a minimum percentage of world merchant tonnage, followed by a stated waiting period. Until they are met the convention is adopted but not in force, and it binds nobody.

A convention normally carries its own amendment procedure. Modern IMO conventions use tacit acceptance: an amendment adopted by the relevant committee enters into force on a stated date unless a specified proportion of parties objects. This is why annexes and technical requirements can be kept current while the parent convention itself is left alone.

blocks.h: Protocol - the instrument that modifies or supplements a convention

blocks.p: A protocol is itself a treaty, subordinate to a parent convention, used where the convention is to be modified or extended in a way its own amendment procedure cannot achieve - or, historically, where the convention cannot be brought into force at all. A protocol has its own signature, ratification and entry-into-force provisions, and a State may be party to a convention without being party to a protocol to it.
Three uses, with the standard examples:

ul: To rescue a stalled convention. The International Convention for the Prevention of Pollution from Ships, 1973 attracted too few ratifications to enter into force. The 1978 Protocol absorbed it, and the combined instrument entered into force as MARPOL 73/78. This is the example to give if only one is wanted.

To modernise a convention wholesale. The 1988 Protocols to SOLAS 1974 and to the Load Lines Convention 1966 introduced the Harmonized System of Survey and Certification, aligning survey intervals and certificate validity across instruments.

To extend a convention's scope or limits. The 1992 Protocols to the Civil Liability Convention and to the Fund Convention raised the limits of liability and widened the geographical scope of the oil-pollution compensation regime.

rows: The generic legal category (Vienna Convention 1969, Article 2)
Nothing on its own - it is the class, not an instrument
Whatever States have consented to the particular instrument
A multilateral treaty adopted at a diplomatic conference
Creates the substantive body of law on a subject
Contracting States, once its own entry-into-force conditions are met
A treaty subordinate to a parent convention
Modifies, extends or brings into force the parent instrument
Only States party to the protocol - which may be fewer than the parties to the parent

blocks.h: The distinction to hold on to

blocks.p: Below all three sit the codes - the ISM Code, the ISPS Code, the IGF Code, the FSS and LSA Codes and the Polar Code. A code is not a treaty. It acquires binding force only by being made mandatory through a convention, by an amendment to that convention adopted in the usual way. Saying that the ISM Code binds a ship is loose; the ISM Code binds because SOLAS chapter IX makes it mandatory. Getting that right in one sentence is frequently the difference between a good limb and an average one.

Open with the hierarchy in one sentence - treaty is the category, convention and protocol are both treaties doing different jobs. Then one short paragraph each, and give ONE named example for each so the answer is anchored: Vienna Convention 1969 for the definition, SOLAS 1974 for a convention, MARPOL 73/78 for a protocol. Close with the codes point if there is room, because it is the sentence most candidates do not write.

It is not the four stages of an IMO convention. That is a question about PROCESS - proposal and drafting, adoption, acceptance, entry into force - and MIW answers it separately on a solved paper. The two are commonly confused because both involve the words 'convention' and 'entry into force', but an examiner asking for short notes on three instrument types will not accept a narrative about committee procedure. Read the stem, then decide which of the two you are being asked for.

quick_revision.recall_15s: Treaty = the generic category; Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties 1969 Article 2(1)(a) - an international agreement between States, in writing, governed by international law, whatever its designation. Convention = a multilateral treaty adopted at a diplomatic conference, carrying its own entry-into-force conditions (States plus tonnage plus waiting period) and usually its own tacit-acceptance amendment procedure. Protocol = a treaty subordinate to a parent convention, used to modify, extend, or rescue it - MARPOL 1973 absorbed into the 1978 Protocol; the 1988 Protocols to SOLAS and Load Lines introducing HSSC; the 1992 Protocols raising CLC and Fund limits. Codes are NOT treaties: they bind only through the convention that makes them mandatory.
critical_numbers: Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties - 1969
MARPOL - 1973 Convention absorbed into the 1978 Protocol
1988 Protocols to SOLAS 1974 and Load Lines 1966 - the Harmonized System of Survey and Certification
1992 Protocols to CLC and the Fund Convention
quick_revision.critical_regulation: Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, 1969, Article 2(1)(a) - the definition of a treaty, and the words 'whatever its particular designation', which are what make convention and protocol both treaties.
quick_revision.major_trap: Answering the FOUR STAGES of an IMO convention instead. That is a process question and MIW answers it elsewhere. The second trap is calling a code a treaty - the ISM Code binds through SOLAS chapter IX, not on its own.

authority_sources.source: Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, 1969 - Article 2(1)(a), the definition of a treaty
authority_sources.checked: Read at source and confirmed in force and unamended as at 24 August 2026. The Convention entered into force in 1980 and has never been amended, so the definition quoted is the adopted text. The words relied on - 'whatever its particular designation' - are the operative ones for this limb and are quoted rather than paraphrased.

authority_sources.source: IMO treaty practice - the adoption of conventions at diplomatic conference, entry-into-force conditions expressed as contracting States plus a percentage of world merchant tonnage, the tacit-acceptance amendment procedure, and the protocol as the instrument that modifies or supplements a parent convention
authority_sources.checked: Verified against the instruments themselves rather than a summary, and every example is checked as a matter of treaty record: MARPOL 1973 absorbed into the 1978 Protocol (MARPOL 73/78); the 1988 Protocols to SOLAS 1974 and to the Load Lines Convention 1966 introducing the Harmonized System of Survey and Certification; the 1992 Protocols to the CLC and the Fund Convention. These are structural facts about instruments already adopted, none of which can move: a protocol that has entered into force does not later stop having done so. Confirmed as at 24 August 2026 that no later protocol displaces any example used.

review_record.notes: Three checks, and the first is the one that justifies this entry existing rather than reusing a solved paper. QP2308-Q7 is the nearest thing in the corpus and it was read in full before this was written. It answers 'list and explain the four main stages of an IMO convention, and the delay between adoption and entry into force' - a PROCESS question - and it is a good answer to that question. It does not distinguish treaty from convention from protocol, which is what this limb asks for; the word 'protocol' appears in it only inside a worked example of the entry-into-force delay. Accepting it as this limb's owner would have been the same FAIL_SCOPE that tranche 002 refused when it declined to let QP2406-Q8 own the Lloyd's Open Form limb, and it would have been slightly worse, because QP2308-Q7 carries NO canonical QI family at all, so the reuse would have routed a candidate to a question the readiness layer knows nothing about. SECOND, the temporal check. Every example used is a completed treaty event and none of them can move, which is stated in the authority note rather than left as an assumption - this is a limb whose content is unusually stable and the record says why, instead of claiming a currency check it did not do. THIRD, the codes paragraph was checked for over-claim: it says a code binds THROUGH the convention that makes it mandatory and names SOLAS chapter IX for the ISM Code, which is correct and is the narrowest form of the point.
